title: The Power of the Cross
english: …men, he recalls the name of Jesus Christ, after whom everyone ought to be called, from the very start of the contest. What he says now is not about doctrines, and he does not blame them for that, but for what we mentioned before, as the words that follow show.

On 1 Corinthians 1:13 and 1:17a: Does Christ have co-heirs, he asks, with whom he has shared you out, you who believe? He did not say, "Was Christ divided?" but, "Did Christ share out with you?" The words that follow show this, for he says, "Was Paul crucified for us?" Christ died for the salvation of the world; none of us did. From this he shows that some wanted to be named after the man who baptized them. This good thing, he says, which the Savior commanded and which brings salvation, would have become a burden to me if you were going to be called after me because I baptized you. How then shall we understand "Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel"? Someone who is not an apostle can baptize, while few held the rank of apostle, and no one could be baptized without first hearing the gospel. So he says, "I was sent to preach the gospel": that is the chief thing, not baptizing. The word "chiefly" is left out here: I was not sent chiefly to baptize. He speaks the same way elsewhere, when he says, "Is it for oxen that God cares?" (1 Corinthians 9:9). That is not because God does not care for them. In the law Moses really does speak about oxen, the beasts that serve farmers. David too says, "Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God" (Psalm 36:6–7). And Solomon says, "The righteous man pities the lives of his beasts" (Proverbs 12:10); how much more God? What then does he mean? That God does not care chiefly for oxen. Here too the sense is elliptical, just like "Christ did not send me to baptize."

On 1 Corinthians 1:17: As he moves on to another charge and comes to another correction, without wholly laying the first aside, he makes the end of the first serve as the opening of the second. "Christ did not send me to baptize" belonged to the first charge, that each of you says, "I am of Paul," and "I am of Apollos." But "not in wisdom of speech" begins a different line of treatment. So he set "to preach the gospel" as both the end of the first matter and the beginning of the second. "So that the cross of Christ may not be emptied": if the preaching is credited to human intelligence and learning, the power of the cross is not shown.

On 1 Corinthians 1:18–20: "The word of the cross." He does not mean the spoken phrase or its utterance, but its power. The deed looks weak, but when you look for its cause, it proves to be a great mystery. "But to us who are being saved it is the power of God." Some want to take "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God" as said of God the Word; so we should note here that he calls the word of the cross the power of God. "For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise" (Isaiah 29:14). The apostle could have been trusted when teaching on his own authority, since he had Christ speaking in him (2 Corinthians 13:3). Even so he also draws on the witness of the Old Testament, and so makes his disciples' conviction stronger. Having used the text "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise," he goes on as if the point were already granted: "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?" The wise man is the Greek's; the scribe is the Jews'.

On 1 Corinthians 1:21: He speaks of two wisdoms. One is the harmony seen in the things God made. The other is the wisdom by which human beings, being rational, have understanding. Since, he says, we did not know God through the understanding we have, nor through the wisdom seen in the things he made, God was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching. What he says is great, and it does not show itself to those who skim past it, for this is how he displays God's power and complete wisdom. The size and beauty of the world, he says, measureless and beyond reach as they are, did not persuade you to know God. Instead you left the Maker and worshiped the very things through which you should have come to know him. To show you the surpassing greatness of his power, God enlightened the world through the confessed weakness of the cross, enlightening people whom creation had not persuaded but only overawed.

On 1 Corinthians 1:22–25: He shows how absurd it is for people to rely on learning and to think that eloquence adorns godliness. One must not answer the Greeks who look for wisdom, he says; one must not even give signs to the Jews who ask for them. Yet signs belong to the Spirit, while wisdom of words belongs to outside learning. If it was not right to give even the wonders of the Spirit to those who asked, how much less the things of outside wisdom (for one is not…
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix-b1): retranslated every clause from the locked Greek (SOURCE_ISSUES item 17). The old English was garbled ('He remembers being named by men', 'Are you not heirs with Christ', 'previously God does not care for the oxen', 'we must not answer not only those seeking wisdom'). Notes now open with the edition's labels: 1:13 and 1:17a, 1:17, 1:18–20, 1:21, 1:22–25. The opening words finish the 1:10 note begun in u01-open. In the 1:17a note the clause ἄνευ τοῦ εὐαγγελισθῆναι καὶ βαπτισθῆναι οὐκ ἐνῆν βαπτισθῆναι has a repeated καὶ βαπτισθῆναι that reads as a copying slip; it is not rendered. title: The Boasting of the Cross vs. Human Pride
english: …to give them to those who put God to the test, but to those who ask in faith), then eloquence is ruled out altogether, as a plot against the glory of the cross. "But we preach Christ crucified," and the rest. Plainly he calls Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God with respect to the word of the cross, as he did above: "For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:18). What follows makes this clearer still. After saying, "but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God," he added, "because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Who would say that God the Word is what is meant by "the weakness of God"? "The foolishness of God" is said of Christ crucified. God the Word is powerful as the Father is, not a power that is a part filling out the Father's substance; and he is wise in the same way. What the visible creation could not achieve, nor angels or archangels coming down from heaven, nor patriarchs and prophets, nor the law given through Moses, nor the voices carried to the people from the midst of the fire, because the choice of the obstinate would not allow it, the foolishness of the cross achieved. That is why Christ crucified is the power of God and the wisdom of God: he accomplished more than the whole dispensation and carried more conviction than all creation. This too is the power of the one who planned it and brought it off: he saved human beings by what counts for nothing and led them to faith in himself.

The second catena form adds: Then he teaches how the preaching seems to be foolishness. They look for signs and wisdom; we preach Christ crucified, the power and wisdom of God, and we promise those who believe salvation from the one who was crucified.
On 1 Corinthians 1:26: He added "according to the flesh" to set it against the Spirit, and the phrase serves in common for the words that follow.

On 1 Corinthians 1:29: "So that no flesh may boast before him": that is, so that they may not credit the success of the preaching to their own advantages. He said "flesh" and not "soul" to belittle human boasting. Why "before him" and not "before men"? Because boasting in our own advantages had been set up against boasting in God: what they ought to have credited to God, they credited to men. That is why he said "before him," for boasting carried on in the sight of the one who sees all things was impious. The whole subject shows that he did not say "before him" with the Coming in view, for he has to deal with people who boast of eloquence and of having baptized, and he is speaking about such matters as these.

On 1 Corinthians 1:30: "But of him you are." Everyone alike says that this is said here of being saved, not in the sense of creation, as it says elsewhere: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh, but of God" (John 1:13). If then we are of him, how can we boast in advantages of our own? Next, "in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom and sanctification and redemption." Human wisdom did not save us, for it was going astray; he himself became our wisdom, to bring us to know God. No human understanding snatched us away; Jesus crucified did. Men did not redeem us. So let the boast be drawn from the one who saved, not from those who were saved.

On 1 Corinthians 2:3–4: I was always afraid that outside learning would puff you up, so I did not use persuasive wisdom. "In weakness," he says, meaning the weakness that comes from persecution, for that is how he always speaks: "in weakness and in fear and in trembling," the weakness caused by those who persecuted me. I showed the fear and trembling I felt for you; I was lowly in everything, so that you might learn from this and not be puffed up. Since he had said "my speech," so that he would not seem to be putting forward the very thing opposed…
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

The old English printed the 1:22–25 notes twice (first-column and second-column forms) and garbled 1:26 ('The fleshly element was added ... give out according to the common'); it printed bare labels '1 Cor 1:26', '1 Cor 1:29', '1 Cor 1:30', '1 Cor 2:3–4'. Doublets collapsed: the second-column forms at edition p. 229,col2 (1:22–24) and p. 230,col2 (1:25) are not reprinted; the first-column form is kept, and the one sentence with no counterpart (the promise of salvation from the crucified one) is printed after 'The second catena form adds:'. The 230,col2 form gives a different reason for the failure of creation, law and prophets: 'because God gives way to the choice of the obstinate' (first form: 'because the choice of the obstinate would not allow it'). Labels now 'On 1 Corinthians 1:26:', '1:29:', '1:30:', '2:3–4:'. The section opens by finishing the 1:22–25 note (so it covers 1:22–25 before 1:26) and ends mid-sentence; u01-rem-close continues it.

title: The distinction of the Spirit and the unity of knowledge
english: …to it, eloquence, he says, "and my preaching was not in persuasive words of wisdom." For there is a wisdom that is not a matter of phrases but of divine knowledge, of the Spirit and of power. The Holy Spirit both supplies a word of wisdom and works wonders, and so he said, "in demonstration of the Spirit and of power." What is said is not yet proof; a wonder carries its proof with it.
The second catena form adds: He shows that he did not preach relying on any human power either.

On 1 Corinthians 2:5: Had he only spoken, he would have been no different from those who use wisdom and trust in their own speech. But by working mighty deeds he showed the strength of God, and the preaching drew its force from there. So he rightly went on, "but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest on human wisdom but on the power of God."

On 1 Corinthians 2:6: That is, not among the learned, but among those who are mature in godliness. He said "among the mature," not "to the mature." Someone who talks to whoever happens along often meets contradiction too. But someone who brings the saving word to the mature and godly does not simply talk: he lays the words up in their souls and stores them there like treasure.

On 1 Corinthians 2:7–8: If it had been hidden, then clearly finding it out was not a task for reasoning; revealing it truly belonged to God. In place of saying that they did not understand, he gives the proof of it: "for if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." By "rulers" he means Pilate and Herod and those around them, and by "the Lord of glory" God made flesh.

On 1 Corinthians 2:9: This quotation is not found in the Old Testament in these words, but in other words with the same meaning. Isaiah says, "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" (Isaiah 53:1) and, "Who shall tell of his generation?" (Isaiah 53:8). And Moses says, "The hidden things belong to the Lord God" (Deuteronomy 29:29). What is hidden with God plainly escaped both eye and heart. We must not think, however, that God revealed the mystery to some without discernment and let others perish in ignorance. We must know, and be convinced, that by his power of foreknowledge he measured out to each what each deserved, for each one's good, and gave it. For he foresees each person's choice even before that person exists.

On 1 Corinthians 2:10: By "the depths of God" he means God's deepest dispensations, which escape our notice. By these words he shows that the Spirit searches, not as one who does not know, but as one who knows. Some say that "Spirit" here means the Father, others the Son, so we must answer both. It cannot mean the Father, for he says, "We have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God" (1 Corinthians 2:12), and no one is from himself; if it were said of God, from whom would God be? One might suspect it means the Son, but he cannot be the one the passage is about. Who would say that God the Word searches in order to learn the things of God? And if they were to say that the Son is taught, how did they fail to see from what follows that the Spirit of God knows as a man's spirit knows what is in him? Besides, the whole passage shows that the Holy Spirit is meant. Notice too that he says the Holy Spirit is "from God," but he did not say the unclean spirit is "from the world," only "of the world." The Paraclete is not a part of God, but the devil, since he came into being, is a part of creation. The Holy Spirit, then, is from God.

On 1 Corinthians 2:11–13: He does not mean that, as our spirit within us is better than we are, so the Spirit in God is better than God, when he says straight away, "For who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit that is in him?" Then what of "in," and of "from God"? "In him" points to a part that fills out the whole man, while "from him" points to the cause. Note too that God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, while a man and the spirit in him are not two persons but one man. So, to show that the Father and the Spirit are exactly the same in knowledge, he compared the knowledge of the spirit in us with the knowledge of the Father and the Spirit. As in us there is no discord within the one and the same spirit, that is, the soul and the mind, and we know what we know, so in the Father and the Holy Spirit there is no discord of knowledge, but sameness. "That we might know the things freely given to us by God": the Spirit gave them, and the mind took hold of them. "Which we also speak." Again he shows something more: not only, he says, not…
